TempoMoE: Identifying and Steering Fast–Slow Thinking Experts for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning

Xiyue Zhang Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Keru Zhou Affiliation: Tsinghua University    Ziyi Wang Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Bing Hu Affiliation: Zhejiang University    Li Wang Affiliation: Wenzhou Business College
Abstract

Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) for complex tasks, yet often overthink easy inputs, increasing token cost and latency, and sometimes degrading accuracy. Existing methods optimize reasoning length during training or impose external control at inference, but leave the underlying reasoning mechanism a black box. We find that fast and slow thinking exhibit distinct expert-routing patterns: holding the input fixed and varying only the prompted reasoning tempo produces stable routing shifts. Suppressing slow-thinking experts shortens the reasoning chain, whereas suppressing fast-thinking experts lengthens it, providing causal evidence that these experts influence reasoning depth. Based on this finding, we propose TempoMoE, a training-free, two-stage framework. It identifies fast- and slow-thinking experts via tempo-contrastive routing analysis and redistributes routing weights within the original top-kk set according to sample difficulty. It amplifies fast-thinking experts and suppresses slow-thinking experts on easy inputs and reverses this adjustment on hard ones, enabling difficulty-adaptive control over reasoning depth. We evaluate TempoMoE on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks. Compared with Vanilla, TempoMoE consistently improves accuracy while reducing output tokens, with accuracy gains of up to 2.6 points and token reductions of up to 35.4%.

1 Introduction

Large reasoning models rely on chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to solve complex tasks Wei et al. (2022). Yet the required reasoning effort varies substantially across inputs. In multimodal tasks, object recognition and multi-step visual mathematics require different levels of computation. However, models may repeatedly verify simple perceptual judgments, increasing token cost and latency and potentially degrading answer quality through redundant reasoning and error accumulation Chen et al. (2025); Sui et al. (2025). Matching computation to input demands is therefore important for efficient multimodal reasoning.

Existing work mitigates overthinking by optimizing reasoning length during training or controlling generation at inference through prompting, token budgets, or decoding heuristics Huang et al. (2024); Xiao and Gan (2025); Diao et al. (2026); Huang et al. (2026a); Yang et al. (2026). The MoE architecture provides a natural entry point for controlling internal computational pathways. Its sparse router dispatches each token to a small subset of experts Shazeer et al. (2017); Fedus et al. (2022), making expert selection and contributions observable and steerable. Prior work has demonstrated expert specialization and the value of targeted expert interventions Wang et al. (2025b); Fayyaz et al. (2026); Hu et al. (2026). However, routing differences between fast and slow thinking for a fixed image and question, and their use for adaptive reasoning control, remain underexplored.

We first conduct a controlled comparison, holding the image and question fixed while varying only the prompted reasoning tempo. We observe stable routing differences during question processing and decoding. Targeted interventions further show that masking the identified slow experts shortens outputs, whereas masking fast experts lengthens them. These findings link expert routing to generation behavior and motivate inference-time expert steering.

Based on these findings, we propose TempoMoE, a training-free, two-stage framework. In the first stage, we identify fast-slow experts through routing comparisons, robustness screening, and intervention tests. In the second stage, TempoMoE estimates input difficulty using prefill routing entropy and continuously adjusts weights within the original top-kk expert set. It favors fast experts on easy inputs and slow experts on hard inputs, without changing the selected expert set or updating model parameters.

We evaluate TempoMoE on three multimodal MoE reasoning models (Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL) across six benchmarks, comparing it with Vanilla and four training-free baselines. Figure 1 summarizes average accuracy and token usage. Compared with Vanilla, TempoMoE improves accuracy while reducing output tokens in all 18 model–benchmark combinations, with accuracy gains of up to 2.6 points and token reductions of up to 35.4%.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    To our knowledge, we are the first to uncover distinct fast- and slow-thinking experts in multimodal MoE reasoning models and provide intervention-based evidence that they influence reasoning depth through role-consistent interventions.

  • •

    We propose TempoMoE, a training-free, two-stage framework that first identifies fast- and slow-thinking experts by contrasting their routing patterns across reasoning tempos, and then adaptively redistributes their routing weights within the original top-kk set according to sample difficulty.

  • •

    We validate TempoMoE across three multimodal MoE reasoning models with distinct routing designs and six benchmarks, showing that it consistently improves accuracy while reducing output tokens.

2 Related Work

Efficient reasoning and overthinking mitigation.

Long chain-of-thought can improve performance on complex tasks but often introduces redundant computation on easy inputs. Existing approaches broadly fall into training-based reasoning-budget optimization and inference-time control. Training-based methods learn concise or sample-adaptive reasoning through length optimization, reinforcement learning, adaptive CoT triggering, or budget prediction Arora and Zanette (2025); Aggarwal and Welleck (2025); Lou et al. (2025); Wu et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025b). Inference-time methods reduce redundant generation through concise intermediate reasoning Xu et al. (2025), prompt-based token budgets or budget forcing Han et al. (2025); Muennighoff et al. (2025), confidence-based early exit Yang et al. (2026); Fu et al. (2025), or suppression of reflection triggers Huang et al. (2026a). These methods highlight the value of adapting computation to input difficulty but primarily control observable generation behaviors, including reasoning budgets, output length, and stopping time, without identifying the internal pathways that produce them.

Fast–slow reasoning in multimodal models.

Fast–slow reasoning has received less attention in multimodal models than in the text-only setting. FAST-GRPO Xiao and Gan (2025), DualMindVLM Lin et al. (2025), and GPRO Diao et al. (2026) adapt the reasoning effort of vision–language models through difficulty-aware training, reasoning-mode selection, or branch routing. Metis-HOME Lan et al. (2025) further incorporates fast–slow reasoning into a trained multimodal MoE architecture. These methods typically rely on retraining or architectural changes and control reasoning through sample-level decisions, discrete modes, or separate branches. They do not explicitly identify whether fast and slow reasoning correspond to distinct internal components.

Expert specialization and routing intervention in MoE.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures provide a natural setting for studying internal mechanisms because sparse routing exposes expert-level computation. They have been increasingly adopted in vision–language models to scale model capacity with limited active computation Lin et al. (2026); Li et al. (2025a); Wu et al. (2024). Recent studies analyze routing patterns to characterize expert specialization across tasks, domains, languages, semantic content, safety properties, and cognitive effort Lo et al. (2025); Olson et al. (2025); Hu et al. (2026); Bandarkar et al. (2026); Lai et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025b). Other approaches manipulate MoE behavior through expert fine-tuning, activation or deactivation, test-time rerouting, and dynamic expert skipping Wang et al. (2024); Fayyaz et al. (2026); Li et al. (2025c); Xu et al. (2026); Huang et al. (2026b). Fast–slow reasoning presents a different setting from task or domain specialization with explicit labels: the same model can exhibit distinct reasoning states for the same image and question. TempoMoE identifies experts associated with these states through controlled reasoning-tempo comparisons, validates their functional roles through targeted interventions, and uses them for difficulty-adaptive reasoning control.

3 Identifying Fast-Slow Experts

TempoMoE consists of two stages: offline expert identification and adaptive modulation during inference, as illustrated in Figure 2. In Stage 1, we identify fast-slow experts across MoE layers by contrasting routing patterns under paired prompts. In Stage 2, TempoMoE estimates input difficulty and performs soft reweighting within the original top-kk expert set. This enables continuous modulation of reasoning effort without updating model parameters or changing the router’s expert selection.

3.1 MoE Routing and Intervention Design

MoE routing.

For token tt at layer ll, the sparse router selects a top-kk expert set 𝒦l,t\mathcal{K}_{l,t} and assigns a routing weight wl,t,ew_{l,t,e} to each selected expert. The output of the routed expert branch is

hl,troute=∑e∈𝒦l,twl,t,e⋅El,e​(hl,tin).h^{\mathrm{route}}_{l,t}=\sum_{e\in\mathcal{K}_{l,t}}w_{l,t,e}\cdot E_{l,e}\!\left(h^{\mathrm{in}}_{l,t}\right). (1)

Shared experts, when present, remain unchanged and are excluded from both expert identification and routing modulation.

Routing intervention design.

We distinguish two intervention levels. In Stage 1, a selection-level intervention masks candidates before top-kk selection to assess their effects on output length. In Stage 2, a weight-level intervention redistributes routing weights after top-kk selection, preserving the original expert set 𝒦l,t\mathcal{K}_{l,t}.

3.2 Fast-Slow Expert Identification

Routing collection.

To identify fast-slow experts, we keep the image and question fixed and use different prompts to elicit fast or slow thinking. Given a multimodal sample x=(I,q)x=(I,q), we construct fast and slow prompt sets 𝒫f\mathcal{P}_{f} and 𝒫s\mathcal{P}_{s} with the same answering objective. We then record the selected experts and routing weights at each MoE layer.

We use three fast prompts requesting direct answers without explicit reasoning and three slow prompts requesting step-by-step reasoning. For example, one pair begins with “Look at the image and answer the question directly” and “Carefully inspect the image and solve the question step by step,” respectively. All prompts specify the same final-answer format: Final answer: <answer>.

We divide the input and generated sequence into image, question, instruction, and decode segments. The instruction segment contains the tempo directive and is used only for diagnostic analysis. The image segment serves as a control because the visual input is identical under both conditions. Candidate identification uses routing differences in the question and decode segments.

Routing differences.

Let wl,t,e​(x,p)w_{l,t,e}(x,p) denote the routing weight of expert ee at layer ll for token tt under prompt pp. Its effective routing contribution is

γl,e(t;x,p)=wl,t,e(x,p)⋅[e∈𝒦l,t(x,p)].\gamma_{l,e}(t;x,p)=w_{l,t,e}(x,p)\cdot\mathbf{1}\!\left[e\in\mathcal{K}_{l,t}(x,p)\right]. (2)

For segment SS, we average this contribution over its tokens, the identification set 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and prompt set 𝒫\mathcal{P}:

Ml,eS​(𝒫)\displaystyle M^{S}_{l,e}(\mathcal{P}) =1|𝒟|​|𝒫|∑x∈𝒟∑p∈𝒫\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}||\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}} (3)
1|𝒯S​(x,p)|​∑t∈𝒯S​(x,p)γl,e​(t,x,p),\displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{S}(x,p)|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{S}(x,p)}\gamma_{l,e}(t;x,p),

where 𝒯S​(x,p)\mathcal{T}_{S}(x,p) denotes the tokens in segment SS. Length normalization prevents longer slow-thinking outputs from receiving disproportionate weight. The routing difference is

Δ​Ml,eS=Ml,eS​(𝒫s)−Ml,eS​(𝒫f).\Delta M^{S}_{l,e}=M^{S}_{l,e}(\mathcal{P}_{s})-M^{S}_{l,e}(\mathcal{P}_{f}). (4)

Positive and negative values indicate preferences for slow and fast prompts, respectively.

Candidate selection.

Let y∈{+1,−1}y\in\{+1,-1\} denote slow and fast thinking, respectively. Bootstrap stability πl,eS,y\pi^{S,y}_{l,e} measures how often an expert appears among the leading candidates in direction yy across resampled datasets. Prompt consistency ρl,eS,y\rho^{S,y}_{l,e} measures the proportion of fast-slow prompt pairs that preserve this directional preference. We filter out experts with small routing differences or negligible average contributions and rank the remaining candidates by

Scorel,eS,y=(y⋅Δ​Ml,eS)⋅πl,eS,y⋅ρl,eS,y.\mathrm{Score}^{S,y}_{l,e}=\left(y\cdot\Delta M^{S}_{l,e}\right)\cdot\pi^{S,y}_{l,e}\cdot\rho^{S,y}_{l,e}. (5)

Intervention screening.

On the identification set, we mask each candidate before top-kk selection and measure the resulting change in output length, including reasoning and final-answer tokens. A slow candidate is retained if masking it shortens the output, whereas a fast candidate is retained if masking it lengthens the output.

The retained candidates form the fast and slow expert sets ℰfast\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{fast}} and ℰslow\mathcal{E}^{\mathrm{slow}}. We normalize their ranking scores within each layer to [0,1][0,1], yielding Al,efastA^{\mathrm{fast}}_{l,e} and Al,eslowA^{\mathrm{slow}}_{l,e} for Stage 2. All other experts receive a profile score of zero. The expert sets and profiles are fixed before held-out validation and downstream evaluation.

4 Difficulty-Adaptive Expert Steering

Given the fast-slow expert profiles identified in Stage 1, TempoMoE estimates input difficulty before decoding and uses it to continuously modulate routing weights within the original top-kk expert set.

Sample difficulty estimation.

TempoMoE estimates input difficulty using routing entropy from the standard prefill pass. We collect routing scores at the last non-padding position of the complete input, which can attend to the full image and question. At each MoE layer, we normalize the native nonnegative routing scores before top-kk selection to obtain a distribution pl,e​(x)p_{l,e}(x) over all routed experts. Shared experts and correction biases used solely for expert selection are excluded. We then compute normalized entropy and average it across layers:

R(x)=−1|ℒ|∑l∈ℒ1log⁡El∑e=1Elpl,e(x)logpl,e(x),R(x)=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{L}|}\sum_{l\in\mathcal{L}}\frac{1}{\log E_{l}}\sum_{e=1}^{E_{l}}p_{l,e}(x)\log p_{l,e}(x), (6)

where ℒ\mathcal{L} denotes the set of MoE layers with at least two routed experts, and ElE_{l} is the number of routed experts at layer ll. Larger values of R⁡(x)R(x) indicate more dispersed routing distributions.

For each model, we construct an empirical percentile mapping FcalF_{\mathrm{cal}} from routing entropy on its calibration set, yielding the difficulty score d⁡(x)=Fcal​(R⁡(x))∈[0,1]d(x)=F_{\mathrm{cal}}(R(x))\in[0,1]. The mapping remains fixed throughout validation and testing. This score serves as a proxy for reasoning effort, not a probability of answer correctness.

Adaptive fast-slow modulation.

We map the difficulty score to a continuous control signal centered at a boundary cc:

s⁡(x)=tanh⁡(d⁡(x)−cτ).s(x)=\tanh\!\left(\frac{d(x)-c}{\tau}\right). (7)

The modulation coefficients for fast and slow experts are

gfast​(x)=−gmax​s​(x),gslow​(x)=gmax​s​(x).g_{\mathrm{fast}}(x)=-g_{\max}s(x),\qquad g_{\mathrm{slow}}(x)=g_{\max}s(x). (8)

Here, cc is the boundary between fast and slow modulation. Across all models we use c=0.5c=0.5, τ=0.25\tau=0.25, and gmax=1.0g_{\max}=1.0, select the top two experts per direction for each model, and apply reweighting only during decoding. The parameter τ>0\tau>0 controls the transition sharpness around the boundary, while gmax≥0g_{\max}\geq 0 determines the maximum modulation strength.

When d⁡(x)<cd(x)<c, TempoMoE amplifies fast experts and suppresses slow experts; the direction is reversed when d⁡(x)>cd(x)>c. The modulation weakens near the boundary, and both coefficients vanish at d⁡(x)=cd(x)=c, leaving the original routing weights unchanged. Thus, the modulation varies continuously with input difficulty rather than switching between two discrete modes.

Soft reweighting within the top-kk set.

We combine the fast-slow gates with the expert profiles to obtain a bias for expert ee at layer ll for each input:

bl,e​(x)=gfast​(x)​Al,efast+gslow​(x)​Al,eslow.b_{l,e}(x)=g_{\mathrm{fast}}(x)A^{\mathrm{fast}}_{l,e}+g_{\mathrm{slow}}(x)A^{\mathrm{slow}}_{l,e}. (9)

For the expert set 𝒦l,t\mathcal{K}_{l,t} selected by the original router, TempoMoE applies this bias and renormalizes the weights within the set:

wl,t,e′=Zl,t​wl,t,e​exp⁡(bl,e​(x))∑j∈𝒦l,twl,t,j​exp⁡(bl,j​(x)),e∈𝒦l,t,w^{\prime}_{l,t,e}=Z_{l,t}\frac{w_{l,t,e}\exp\!\left(b_{l,e}(x)\right)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{K}_{l,t}}w_{l,t,j}\exp\!\left(b_{l,j}(x)\right)},\qquad e\in\mathcal{K}_{l,t}, (10)

where wl,t,ew_{l,t,e} is the original routing weight and Zl,t=∑j∈𝒦l,twl,t,jZ_{l,t}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{K}_{l,t}}w_{l,t,j} is the total routing mass before reweighting. This operation changes only the relative contributions of the selected experts, preserving both the expert set and its total routing mass. Experts not identified as fast or slow receive zero bias, and shared experts remain unchanged.

Online computational cost.

The difficulty score is computed once per input during the standard prefill pass and remains fixed throughout decoding. This requires neither trial generation nor an additional model forward pass. Normalization and entropy calculation use FP32 and add O⁡(∑l∈ℒEl)O(\sum_{l\in\mathcal{L}}E_{l}) operations, plus one percentile mapping lookup. Reweighting is applied only during decoding. It adds O⁡(k)O(k) scalar operations per routed MoE layer and generated token, with no additional expert feed-forward computation.

5 Experiments

Experiments span three multimodal MoE reasoning models with distinct routing designs and six benchmarks covering a range of reasoning demands. We examine TempoMoE’s trade-off between accuracy and efficiency across models and tasks, with ablations isolating the contributions of expert identification, difficulty-adaptive modulation, and top-kk-preserving soft reweighting.

5.1 Experimental Setup

Models.

TempoMoE is evaluated on three multimodal MoE reasoning models: Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking-2506 Kimi Team (2025), Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Thinking Bai et al. (2025), and ERNIE-4.5-VL-28B-A3B-Thinking Baidu ERNIE Team (2025). Their differences in expert count, routing sparsity, and shared-expert design allow us to assess generalization across distinct MoE routing architectures. All experiments use the corresponding Thinking checkpoints with BF16 inference, while shared generation settings remain fixed across methods.

Benchmarks.

The benchmark suite comprises six multimodal tasks spanning direct visual understanding to multi-step reasoning. OCRBench Liu et al. (2024), RealWorldQA xAI (2024), and ChartQA Masry et al. (2022) emphasize visual recognition and information extraction; MMStar Chen et al. (2024) jointly evaluates multimodal perception and reasoning; MathVista Lu et al. (2024) targets visual mathematical reasoning, whereas MMMU Yue et al. (2024) evaluates multidisciplinary knowledge and reasoning.

Baselines.

We compare TempoMoE with Vanilla and four representative training-free baselines. NoThinking (Ma et al., 2025) skips explicit thinking, TALE (Han et al., 2025) allocates an input-dependent reasoning budget, and NoWait (Wang et al., 2025a) suppresses redundant reflection during decoding. RICE (Wang et al., 2025b) identifies cognitive experts through associations between expert activations and thinking-related tokens. It amplifies their routing weights at inference time, providing a baseline for expert-level reasoning control.

Metrics.

We report accuracy (Acc, %) and average output tokens (Tok), including both the reasoning segment and the final answer. Tok serves as a proxy for autoregressive generation cost. For difficulty-stratified analysis, we divide evaluation samples into Easy and Hard using the calibration-set median of d⁡(x)d(x), without evaluation labels. This split is used only for analysis; online modulation still follows the continuous control signal centered at 0.50.5 in Equation (7).

5.2 Main Results

Expert identification.

We use 600 samples (100 per benchmark) for expert identification and difficulty calibration. Each sample is run with three fast- and three slow-thinking prompts, yielding 3,600 routing runs per model. A separate 600-sample set, disjoint from both the identification and main evaluation sets, is used for intervention validation under the standard Thinking prompt with Vanilla, fast-expert masking, and slow-expert masking. Table 1 reports the identification and intervention results.

Across all three models, masking fast-thinking experts increases output length, whereas masking slow-thinking experts shortens it. High bootstrap stability and prompt consistency further support robust expert identification and role-consistent intervention effects.

Performance across models.

Table 2 reports complete results for TempoMoE, Vanilla, and the four training-free baselines. Compared with Vanilla, TempoMoE improves accuracy while reducing output tokens in all 18 model–benchmark combinations. When macro-averaged over the six benchmarks, it outperforms Vanilla on both metrics for all three models. At the benchmark level, accuracy improves by up to 2.6 points and output tokens decrease by up to 35.4%.

Despite differences in expert count, top-kk configuration, and shared-expert design, Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL exhibit the same trend, indicating that the gains are not tied to a particular MoE routing architecture.

Baseline comparison.

NoThinking, TALE, and NoWait mainly reduce computation by shortening, bypassing, or constraining the explicit reasoning process. When macro-averaged over the six benchmarks, NoThinking reduces output tokens by more than 60% for each model but lowers average accuracy by 4.0–9.4 points. TALE and NoWait are less aggressive, yet their average accuracy also remains below Vanilla.

Compared with RICE, TempoMoE achieves higher accuracy in all 18 settings. Across the three models, it improves macro-averaged accuracy by 2.5–3.9 points with comparable or lower macro-averaged output token counts. TempoMoE also improves both metrics over RICE in 10 of the 18 settings. For example, on MathVista with Qwen3-VL, TempoMoE improves accuracy from RICE’s 76.5% to 82.9% with similar output lengths. Compared with Vanilla, TempoMoE improves accuracy from 81.9% to 82.9% while reducing the average output from 1350.7 to 1172.9 tokens, demonstrating a favorable trade-off between accuracy and generation cost.

Task analysis.

The size of the efficiency gain varies by task. On OCRBench, which emphasizes visual perception and direct recognition, TempoMoE improves accuracy over Vanilla by 1.4–2.6 points and reduces output tokens by 21.4–35.4% across the three models. It also achieves higher accuracy than RICE on this benchmark for all three models.

On the more reasoning-intensive MathVista and MMMU, TempoMoE also improves both metrics over Vanilla. Across the six corresponding settings, accuracy increases by 0.5–1.4 points while output tokens decrease by 7.9–19.5%. Since the original outputs on these benchmarks are considerably longer, even moderate relative reductions yield meaningful absolute savings. On RealWorldQA, ChartQA, and MMStar, token reductions vary by model, while accuracy improves consistently over Vanilla.

Figure 3 illustrates this effect on a visual localization question. Vanilla repeatedly checks the white lamp’s location and describes surrounding details before reaching the correct answer. TempoMoE gives the same correct answer, “left,” while reducing thinking tokens from 113 to 35, a reduction of approximately 69%. This example illustrates how TempoMoE reduces repeated checking while preserving answer correctness.

5.3 Ablation Study

We conduct ablation studies to evaluate the contributions of expert identification, difficulty-adaptive modulation direction, and top-kk-preserving soft reweighting. The results are reported in Table 3.

Random Experts replaces the identified fast- and slow-thinking experts with the same number of randomly selected experts from the same layers, matched by routing usage, while retaining the same modulation rule. Fixed-Fast and Fixed-Slow retain the sample-dependent modulation magnitude but force the modulation direction toward fast or slow thinking, respectively, for all inputs. Hard Mask uses the same identified experts and difficulty-conditioned direction but masks the target experts before top-kk selection instead of softly reweighting them after selection.

Expert identification.

Random Experts leaves the average output-token count nearly unchanged from Vanilla but substantially lowers overall accuracy. Compared with Random Experts, TempoMoE improves overall accuracy by 4.7 points and reduces the average output by 64.1 tokens. This shows that the gains of TempoMoE depend on the identified fast- and slow-thinking experts rather than generic routing perturbations.

Adaptive direction.

Fixed-Fast matches TempoMoE on easy samples but lowers accuracy on hard samples by 8.7 points, whereas Fixed-Slow matches TempoMoE on hard samples but generates 109.5 more tokens on average on easy samples. Since both variants retain the sample-dependent modulation magnitude, these results isolate the effect of adapting the modulation direction. TempoMoE selects the direction according to sample difficulty, achieving the highest overall accuracy while reducing output tokens. A single global direction therefore cannot accommodate inputs with different reasoning demands.

Soft reweighting.

Hard Mask underperforms Vanilla in accuracy and produces longer outputs, indicating that changing expert selection before top-kk routing is overly disruptive. TempoMoE preserves the original expert set and redistributes routing weights, providing less disruptive control.

6 Conclusion

We present TempoMoE, a training-free, two-stage framework for identifying and modulating fast- and slow-thinking experts in multimodal MoE reasoning models. Through controlled reasoning-tempo comparisons, robustness screening, and role-consistent interventions, we uncovered expert routing patterns associated with different reasoning tempos and demonstrated causal effects on output length, consistent with their tempo-associated roles. Building on these findings, TempoMoE performs difficulty-adaptive reweighting within the original top-kk expert set, without updating model parameters or altering expert selection. Experiments across three models with distinct MoE routing designs and six benchmarks show that TempoMoE consistently improves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off, with accuracy gains of up to 2.6 points and output-token reductions of up to 35.4%. More broadly, our results show that expert-level routing mechanisms can serve not only as explanatory tools, but also as actionable control signals for efficient and adaptive multimodal reasoning.

Limitations

TempoMoE requires access to internal expert routing and model-specific offline expert identification and difficulty calibration, and therefore primarily applies to multimodal MoE models with accessible internal routing. We evaluate TempoMoE on three models and six benchmarks; its performance across a broader range of model architectures and task distributions remains to be explored. Expert profiles and calibration mappings may depend on the data and prompt formulations, and recalibration may be needed under substantial distribution shifts. We use output token counts as a proxy for generation cost, while actual runtime efficiency also depends on the inference implementation and hardware environment.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
